articles.title: Eight Sleep announces the Pod 6, its newest smart mattress cover - Engadget
articles.text:
Eight Sleep announces the Pod 6, its newest smart mattress cover
There are more biometric sensors, better temperature controls and a version for solo use.
Eight Sleep just unveiled the Pod 6, its latest and greatest smart sleep system. The company says these new models have been "rebuilt from the ground up" and represent its "most significant hardware launch to date."
There are a bunch of upgrades here when compared to the Pod 5. The hub has been completely redesigned and is now small enough to fit under most bed frames. It pumps temperature-controlled water inside the included mattress cover to keep things comfortable. Eight Sleep says the Pod 6 offers "the fastest temperature response" of any of its products, as it should be around 20 percent faster when adjusting the temp to handle night sweats and chills.
The Pod 6 line also includes 18 biometric sensors, compared to just two with the Pod 5. These sensors track a sleeper's heart rate, breath rate, heart rate variability, snoring, sleep stages and more, all without the need of a wearable. This information is available with a proprietary app.
The sensors also feed the AI engine and the Autopilot system, which automatically adjust the mattress cover based on sleep stage and ambient temperature. The company boasts that these sensors can distinguish two people sleeping close together or separate a human sleeper's signal from a pet on the bed.
Finally, there's a new smaller size to accommodate solo sleepers. This doesn't change the functionality at all, other than the fact there's no dual-zone temperature regulation system in place. So what's the benefit? It's cheaper. As always, standard sizes accommodate two people's individual needs simultaneously.
Now here's the rub, and it's the same rub as always with Eight Sleep's products. The Pod 6 is extremely expensive. Even the "budget-friendly" solo model starts at $2,000. These prices balloon all the way up to $3,000, depending on mattress size. Every single model also requires a subscription to its Autopilot program, which costs $17 to $25 per month.
It's worth remembering that the Pod 6 isn't a mattress, despite being priced like one. It's a smart sleep system consisting of a hub and a mattress cover. It's available for purchase right now.

articles.title: ChatGPT mobile app gets voice-based agentic features | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI announced on Wednesday that it is bringing voice-based agentic features to mobile, allowing users to trigger workflows like drafting documents or summarizing emails.
Plus and Pro users will be able to use the Work tab on their phone to create a document, draft an email, or summarize Slack messages, for instance. These subscribers can do things like build sites, create presentations, use the cloud browser, and also access other areas like finances in ChatGPT. Free and Go users, meanwhile, will get to work with plugins and connected apps.
OpenAI said ChatGPT’s voice conversations will have richer text output. Plus, users will be able to switch between text and voice easily. They can also start working on a conversation on the go and resume it on desktop.
The feature arrives as an increasing number of users are turning to voice to issue commands to AI assistants for complex tasks.
In July, OpenAI launched its new conversational model GPT-Live, and later the company integrated it with the desktop app to let users use their voice to complete tasks in the Work tab or build apps in the Codex tab. The new rollout brings similar capabilities to the mobile app.
Recently, Anthropic made the handoff between mobile and desktop easier and also merged its Cowork and Chat interface. But OpenAI is still keeping chat and workspaces separate.

articles.title: Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses
articles.text:
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket.
Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses
The new Meta VR Glasses offer immersive experiences in a shape that’s much easier to actually wear.
The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at Meta’s campus this week, and as Meta walked me through some familiar VR demos like watching content, playing a game, and working from multiple screens, I was impressed by how much lighter the whole experience felt. Some of that was about the literal weight, as the glasses come in at just 100g, far less than the Quest 3’s 515g. But there was also something lighter in a more intangible way: the glasses form factor made the headset seem like something I could easily jump in and out of instead of being a whole cumbersome commitment with big head straps. It felt like a lightweight Vision Pro, and is perhaps a better execution of some of what Apple wanted to do with that device.
To keep things light, the VR Glasses’ display and the sensors are all you actually wear on your face. The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.
The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. On the front of the glasses are two cameras for color passthrough, letting you see through to the world around you. The headset comes in small and large sizes to offer different options for width, though they cost the same.
You primarily use your eyes and hand gestures to control the glasses. You just look at elements onscreen to navigate, and the OS will highlight what your eyes are looking at using two pairs of eye-tracking cameras. To select something that’s highlighted, you can pinch your thumb and pointer finger together, and to scroll around, you make a fist and move your thumb around the top of your hand. It feels similar to the gestures from the Meta Ray-Ban Display, but those require a neural wristband; the VR Glasses instead use six external cameras to follow your hands.
Based on my demos, I think the VR Glasses will be best for entertainment because of the big virtual screen. Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court. I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic. In the entire VR environment around the screen showing the film, there were graphics that thematically lined up with what was actually happening onscreen that also changed as the clip went on; when a huge energy beam appeared at a major moment in the film featuring Thor, I saw one shoot out at the top of the VR environment, too. Meta says that VR enhanced versions of Avengers: Infinity War and Star Wars: A New Hope will be available when the VR Glasses launch.
Gaming remains a major use case, too. Meta showed me a new mode for Beat Saber called Flux that supports playing with hands (though it will work with the Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, too). Instead of waving virtual sabers to hit blocks in time with the music, like in the original, Flux tasked me with moving my hands, which were each surrounded by balls of energy connected by pulsing electricity, to break through flying poles and smash targets. It makes sense when you play it, and the one song I played was really enjoyable. The VR Glasses will have more than 75 games at launch that will support the new hands-first experience (including a VR version of Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Dual Destinies launching in 2027), but they’ll also support the entire current Quest app catalog and can connect to Touch Plus controllers (and Bluetooth controllers).
Meta is also pitching this as a way to browse apps and do some work, and I can see the vision. In one demo, I used the glasses to mirror three windows from a nearby laptop. You’ll be able to connect wirelessly to computers or other devices with a USB-C connection, which could be useful if you want more screen real estate for work. My favorite demo from my whole session was actually one about typing. While using a special version of Instagram made for the VR Glasses, I was prompted to leave a comment on a picture, but I was able to type that comment and navigate the app using a virtual keyboard and trackpad that appeared after I laid my hands flat on the table. To my surprise, the virtual keyboard and trackpad were actually good. Of course, the experience wasn’t as speedy as using a physical keyboard and mouse, but in a pinch for a short message or email, I think it could be quite useful. (I should note it’s not technically new; Meta introduced this for Quest headsets earlier this year, and I haven’t tried it on those devices.)
The glasses cost $1,299.99 and will go on sale in spring 2027. That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them. I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.
Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge. But as tech companies chase the next big hardware category, however, a new form factor is starting to emerge: something that’s more capable than most smart glasses but less overbearing than a full-on VR headset. Google and Xreal are teaming up on XR glasses. Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too. The VR Glasses represent another fascinating idea of what a computer on your head can be.

articles.title: Zendesk and Sierra say per-seat pricing is over for AI agents
articles.text:
Zendesk CEO Tom Eggemeier and Sierra co-founder Clay Bavor said on Wednesday that per-seat pricing for software is on its way out. They spoke at HumanX in Amsterdam. In separate sessions, both said customers should pay for AI agents only when the agents get a job done.
“Unequivocally: seats are dead,” Eggemeier said.
Both sell AI agents for customer service. They spoke as software stocks recover from what investors called the SaaSpocalypse. Things looked “pretty dark early in the year,” Bavor said. Software stocks have since come back a bit off the lows.
Paying for a result
Zendesk moved to outcome-based pricing for its AI agents in August 2024, Eggemeier said. He called it the first company to do so. It now plans to drop seats across its business, with announcements due in three to six months. For many companies, pricing by interaction will be a first step, he said.
Sierra charges only when its agents resolve an issue or make a sale, Bavor said. He put it in numbers. If a company pays one euro to resolve a case that costs ten in a call centre, it saves nine euros each time.
“The ROI is so clear you don’t have to do fuzzy envelope math about productivity gains,” Bavor said.
Sierra originates more than $1bn of new mortgages a month for companies such as Rocket Mortgage, he said. It serves almost half of the Fortune 50 and one in three of the world’s largest banks. OpenAI has also started outcome-based pricing for some customers.
Zendesk defines an outcome with each customer, Eggemeier said. In support, it is usually a problem solved without a human. For a UK used-car marketplace, it can mean an AI agent closing a £500 gap on a sale.
Who survives
The two differed on what keeps a software company alive. Coding agents such as Opus 4.5 and Codex 5.2 made software easier to build, Bavor said. Agents are also separating the interface from the data behind it. Companies with authoritative data, such as SAP in supply chains, hold up best, he said.
Eggemeier gave three tests. Companies must treat AI as both an existential threat and an opportunity. This shift will take three to five years, he said, not the ten to twenty of the move to the cloud. They must change their business model. They must also send people into the field to guide customers.
“If you’re still on seats in two or three years, I believe your company will struggle,” Eggemeier said.
Agents talking to agents
Zendesk expects AI agents to handle more than 80% of interactions within about three years, with humans handling the rest. Eggemeier said total interactions will grow sharply, and AI agent to AI agent interactions will pass 50% within two years. He uses Meta’s Muse himself, he said. Over the weekend, Zendesk tested whether a personal agent could buy its software online. It found a couple of gaps.
Bavor said personal agents such as Meta’s Muse will soon talk directly to business agents, within about six months. Most Sierra customers move staff to higher-value work rather than cutting them, he said. Some have created a new role, the “AI architect”, who coaches the agents.
Both moderators raised the Hugging Face incident, in which OpenAI agents reached Hugging Face. Bavor said Sierra’s customer-facing agents have far more limited tools than agents that can write arbitrary code. Eggemeier called cybersecurity his most worrying topic as CEO.
“Right now, offensive AI-agent hacking capability is ahead of defensive capability,” Eggemeier said.
Two of Zendesk’s three main AI hubs are in Berlin and Lisbon, Eggemeier said. The gap between San Francisco and Europe in AI has shrunk to weeks, he said. What worries him more is the growing gap with places like Ohio and Kentucky, where he is from.

articles.title: Volkswagen brings Tetris and other games to its infotainment displays - Engadget
articles.text:
Volkswagen brings Tetris and other games to its infotainment displays
AirConsole is available in 2027 vehicles and will launch with 20 games.
As arguably the most unimprovable video game of all time, it's unsurprising that Tetris has been playable on nearly any console you can name. And if you drive a 2027 Volkswagen, you can add your car to that extensive list.
The iconic puzzler is one of 20 games that feature in Volkswagen's AirConsole in-vehicle entertainment offering, with Pac-Man Championship Edition and Uno Car Party also named in the press release. Developed by N-Dream, the platform is baked into the infotainment system on 2027 Atlas, Atlas Cross Sport, Tiguan, Golf GTI, Golf R and ID vehicles.
Once you've booted up the game you want to play on the display, you use your phone as a wireless controller, but it isn't clear how many devices will be supported at launch. It doesn't sound like there will be any other compatible peripherals, so you will need to use a smart device to play games, or several for multiplayer.
Volkswagen says that some games will have ambient lighting integration with certain vehicles, which will correspond with whatever's happening in the game you're playing. There's also a custom Volkswagen version of Pac-Man, which replaces the familiar power pellets with Volkswagen logos, while fruit pickups become cars. That all sounds a bit sacrilegious to me, but fans of weird crossovers will be happy.
To access AirConsole, you'll need to be signed up to Volkswagen's In-Vehicle Premium service, which also includes Wi-Fi hotspot support, exclusive navigation features and various other connected experiences. Most 2027 vehicles come with three complimentary months of the service, but if you want to keep playing Tetris in the parking lot after that (and, sensibly, you do need to be parked to access the game library), you'll need to pay $149 per year for the privilege.

articles.title: Lãi suất ngân hàng hôm nay 23/9/2026: Bổ sung lãi suất tiền gửi từ 50 tỷ
articles.text:

articles.title: Even Americans who use AI every day are worried about it | TechCrunch
articles.text:
People across the world are increasingly turning to AI for everyday tasks, from looking up recipes and doing their homework to researching work projects or making presentations.
But using AI every day doesn’t necessarily mean people are feeling comfortable with its implications for the world: About 68% of Americans who use AI daily are worried about it, according to a new survey conducted by opinion research firm Gallup, and concern about the tech skews even higher among people who use it less frequently.
Coming at a time of intense debate around the dangers of AI, quick developments around AI safety, the implications of AI going rogue, and accusations of anticompetitive behavior, these findings complicate the notion that adoption can serve as a straightforward measure of public enthusiasm for AI.
Commissioned by Microsoft, the Gallup study currently has results from 37 countries, where researchers polled about 1,000 people in each country between April and July. The project will eventually span 140 countries. Notably, India, a large population of tech users, is not currently part of the reported results, nor are Australia and Malaysia.
The findings appear to put the U.S. at the anxious end of an international chart even as people in other parts of the world expect the technology to improve their lives. According to Gallup, Western countries are most concerned about AI, with the United States leading in anxiety — 74% of Americans reported feelings of worry, and only 36% expect AI to mostly help the country.
Other wealthy Western countries showed a similar mix of relatively frequent use and concern. In Canada, for example, 29% of those surveyed reported using AI daily, and of those, more than half expressed concerns about the impact of the technology. Overall, 64% of Canadians aware of AI said it worried them.
There’s certainly been a growing wave of discontent around AI, with tech companies laying off hundreds of thousands of employees in order to invest in AI, shrinking entry-level openings, life-ending cases of AI psychosis, and dire warnings from AI leaders like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who warned that the tech will wipe out jobs en masse.
The survey paints a different picture in the rest of the world, however. In Singapore, which had the highest portion of daily users in the study (46%), more than 80% of those aware about AI expect the tech to improve their everyday lives, and 77% think it’ll help the country. In China, where 35% of people report using AI daily, most people expect it to help the country. The story is similar in Israel.
Still, optimism about AI doesn’t necessarily appear to translate to trust in the tech’s accuracy. According to Gallup, people who use AI daily were generally more trusting of its results, especially in high-adoption countries like Singapore, Israel, and China, while less frequent users remain skeptical across the board. In the U.S., only 45% of daily users expressed that level of confidence. Altogether, only 36% (median) of the people surveyed said they trust AI’s results a lot.
Overall, though, Gallup reports that positivity about AI outweighs negative sentiments: In 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, people mostly reported feeling curious about the tech, with a fewer number saying they felt happy or excited. Only about 32% of those surveyed said they felt worried about AI. Positive emotions seem to be most common in China (90%), Singapore (89%), and Kenya (87%).
It’s not clear how much sentiment in some countries, especially China, might have changed since the survey ended in July, as the pace of AI development has lately burgeoned into a matter of international importance. AI safety is one of the major topics on the table for discussion when U.S. president Donald Trump and Chinese premier Xi Jinping meet on Thursday.
Notably, China’s head of the Ministry of State Security, Chen Yixin, wrote in a recent article that AI will have “a systemic impact on the political and security environment,” and could threaten China’s “political security, institutional security, and ideological security.”
“One of the clearest findings is that attitudes toward AI are multidimensional. People can be curious about AI, expect it to be beneficial and use it frequently while still being worried about it. Similarly, they can see considerable potential in AI while remaining skeptical about whether the information it provides is accurate,” Pablo Diego-Rosell, senior scientist at Gallup, told TechCrunch.
While the report paints a picture of optimism colored by some concern, it’s nevertheless true that AI worries are increasingly becoming part of public discourse. People who rely on AI for day-to-day tasks may end up supporting tougher rules or resisting its use in hiring, healthcare, education, or government. And there’s certainly an argument to be made that training and serving AI models can harm the climate, and their unregulated use can disrupt cybersecurity, diminish content ownership, upset the creative arts fields, or harm data privacy.
At the end of the day, the report suggests that greater exposure alone will not resolve the unease around the technology. Still, given the amount of money that’s being invested, AI will likely continue proliferating even as disputes rage around where it belongs and what limits should be placed around it.

articles.title: Muse is coming to Meta smart glasses
articles.text:
Just a couple of weeks after launching Muse, Meta announced that it’s “working on” bringing the agent to its smart glasses, including the new glasses it unveiled at Meta Connect. Users will be able to activate Muse from their glasses by saying its name and ask it to handle tasks like guiding a workout, logging meals, or helping them shop for products they’re looking at.
Muse is coming to Meta smart glasses
Meta’s AI agent is arriving on its glasses alongside a wave of new accessibility, camera, and navigation features.
Muse is just one of several major updates coming to Meta’s glasses. They’re also getting some new accessibility features, like a Hearing Enhancement feature Meta says is “FDA-cleared software for adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss.” It will be available later this year with a Meta One subscription or as a $149 add-on for compatible glasses. Meta AI will also be able to give “more context-rich answers” when users ask the glasses what they’re looking at, potentially making Meta’s glasses more effective for helping blind and low-vision users interpret their surroundings. A new audio customization feature will also allow users to shift their smart glasses’ volume between their left and right ears, including sending all audio to one side.
Meta’s introducing some new audio and photo features as well, including Dolby Atmos Capture, which will allow users to record videos with 360-degree spatial audio. A new Dynamic Photo feature automatically captures multiple frames when you take a photo with Meta’s glasses, then uses Meta AI to suggest the best frame from each batch.
The Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are getting the new “Hologram” feature Meta announced for its new VR Glasses, which it says is “a photorealistic digital version of your face for calls from Meta Ray-Ban Display” that “infers” your expression using your voice. The feature’s “rolling out in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”
A couple new heads-up navigation features are coming to the Meta Ray-Ban Display as well. Starting later this month, users in the US and Canada will have an option to use their voice to ask for real-time cycling or public transit directions. The Meta Ray-Ban Display will also start using “the world in front of you rather than street signs in turn-by-turn walking directions,” like referencing a house, car, or landmark the glasses detect. A few other new features are on the way for the Display glasses, including an option for editing photos directly on the glasses’ display, a new “Explore” app for finding new apps, an improved calendar, and mirroring for phone notifications.

articles.title: 60.000 con gà, vịt chết sau lũ, chủ trang trại ở Thanh Hoá thiệt hại tới 10 tỷ đồng
articles.text:
Ngày 22/9, tại trang trại Hồ Mơ Xanh ở thôn Yên Hòa, xã Nông Cống, hàng chục công nhân tất bật thu gom xác gia cầm, dọn bùn đất, vệ sinh chuồng trại và đưa số gia cầm còn sống đến khu vực cao ráo.
Chị Phan Thanh Huyền, chủ trang trại, cho biết đêm 16/9, nước lũ bất ngờ dâng cao, tràn vào khu vực chăn nuôi khiến trang trại mất điện, hệ thống thông gió và làm mát ngừng hoạt động.
Nhiệt độ trong chuồng tăng cao, đàn gia cầm bị sốc nhiệt và chết hàng loạt chỉ trong thời gian ngắn.
“Vào thời điểm đó, khi nước lên cao, hệ thống quạt thông gió ngừng hoạt động. Gia đình đã tìm cách phá tường, đưa các ô nuôi lên vị trí cao hơn để cứu đàn gia cầm nhưng không thể ngăn thiệt hại. Chỉ trong thời gian ngắn, hàng chục nghìn con gà, vịt chết hàng loạt do ngạt khí”, chị nói.
Trang trại của gia đình chị Huyền bắt đầu chăn nuôi quy mô nhỏ từ nhiều năm trước. Hơn 2 năm trở lại đây, gia đình đầu tư mở rộng, phát triển đàn với chi phí đầu tư cả chục tỷ đồng.
Theo chủ trang trại, trước khi xảy ra lũ, đàn gà, vịt tại đây khoảng 140.000 con. Sau đợt mưa lũ, ít nhất 60.000 con đã bị chết, trọng lượng bình quân 1,5-2 kg/con, tương đương hơn 40% tổng đàn ban đầu. Số gia cầm sống sót vẫn tiếp tục chết do ảnh hưởng của ngạt khí và bị ngâm nước trước đó.
Tổng thiệt hại ban đầu được chủ trang trại ước tính khoảng 7-10 tỷ đồng.
Chị Huyền cho hay, thiệt hại không chỉ đến từ số gia cầm chết mà còn bao gồm máy móc, hệ thống điện, chuồng trại và các chi phí phát sinh để khắc phục hậu quả.
Tại trang trại, xác gà, vịt được thu gom liên tục. Đến ngày 21/9, nước lũ cơ bản đã rút hết, gia đình chị phải thuê thêm nhân công thời vụ để dọn dẹp, với tiền công khoảng 500.000-1 triệu đồng/người/ngày.
“Công việc đặc biệt vất vả bởi số lượng xác gia cầm lớn, trong khi nền chuồng vẫn còn ẩm ướt, nhiều khu vực ngập bùn và nước bẩn. Gia đình cũng đang thu gom xác gia cầm, tập kết và xử lý theo hướng dẫn của cơ quan chức năng nhằm hạn chế ô nhiễm và nguy cơ phát sinh dịch bệnh”, chị nói.
Theo chủ trang trại, thiệt hại lớn khiến bài toán khôi phục sản xuất trở nên khó khăn. Gia đình đang vay vốn ngân hàng và dự kiến phải xin giãn nợ để có thời gian phục hồi.
Đại diện UBND xã Nông Cống cho biết địa phương đang hướng dẫn các hộ chăn nuôi bị ảnh hưởng vệ sinh chuồng trại, tiêu độc, khử trùng và xử lý gia cầm chết, nhằm hạn chế nguy cơ phát sinh dịch bệnh.
Việc tái đàn được yêu cầu thực hiện từng bước, bảo đảm các điều kiện an toàn dịch bệnh.
Tại trang trại Hồ Mơ Xanh, do số lượng gia cầm chết quá lớn, chính quyền đang tiếp tục giám sát, hỗ trợ việc thu gom, xử lý và vệ sinh chuồng trại; đồng thời phối hợp với gia đình tìm giải pháp cứu chữa đàn gia cầm còn lại, từng bước ổn định sản xuất.

articles.title: US rejects global AI governance at UN Security Council
articles.text:
The United States is rejecting any global governance of advanced AI, telling the UN Security Council in New York today that each country should regulate the technology itself.
Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, delivers the US statement after the meeting’s four briefers from science and industry.
“The frontier of intelligence is advancing rapidly. That is not a reason to pause its further development or to constrain it with new global governance structures,” Kratsios says.
Throughout his statement, he refers to advanced AI as superintelligence.
The US, which he calls the leader in the field, has worked with frontier labs to test new models and has set up cybersecurity clearinghouses to coordinate on vulnerabilities, he says.
Washington is committed to dialogue on emerging technologies, Kratsios adds, but talks at the UN and elsewhere must not drift towards global governance.
“As President Trump said before the General Assembly yesterday, the United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a global scheme of control of superintelligence,” he says.
He points instead to the Carolina Principles, agreed by G20 innovation ministers in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, this month. Countries should keep national control over how they govern emerging technologies, he says.
“The American people’s representatives will legislate and regulate on the American people’s behalf. You should do the same for your people,” Kratsios tells the Council.
The US offer to other countries is its technology. Through its exports program, American companies will help partners build secure infrastructure and their own AI capability, he says.
“If you take the risks and benefits of superintelligence seriously, the most important thing you can do is to develop your country’s ability to understand and use it,” Kratsios says.
The Council and similar bodies, he argues, should focus on sharing best practice to build that capacity at home rather than creating a global regulatory scheme.
“A prosperous future will not be secured by a global regulator,” he says.
His position sets Washington apart from Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Clément Delangue, the heads of OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face.
Each called for international standards or disclosure rules earlier in the meeting, but Yoshua Bengio went further, calling for frontier AI to be licensed.

articles.title: The pros and cons of using a password manager over an authenticator app - Engadget
articles.text:
The pros and cons of using a password manager over an authenticator app
Convenience vs. maximum isolation: Here's how to choose where your verification codes live.
When it comes to keeping your online accounts safe and sound, two-factor authentication (2FA) has been a standard recommendation from security experts worldwide for years. As more and more people adopt 2FA, one question keeps coming up: Should you store your authentication codes inside your password manager or keep them in a dedicated authenticator app?
The idea that your login should rely on two separate factors is a fundamental security principle. Password managers offer one approach, while authenticator apps offer another. Each comes with real trade-offs that aren't always obvious at first glance. While they're both designed to protect you, they work in completely different ways.
Two-factor authentication is built on the simple idea that if someone steals your password, they still won't be able to get into your account without a second piece of proof of your identity. Some apps will send you a text message with a one-time-use code, some will make a number pop on your phone screen, a few will email you a code, while others will ask if you'd rather use a special code generated by an authenticator app.
A password manager, on the other hand, brings both factors into the same vault, trading some of that separation for convenience. Neither approach is wrong, and each reflects a different set of priorities, like how much friction you're willing to accept, how you manage devices and what you're most worried about losing access to. Understanding how these tools work, how they differ and what you need is the recipe for finding the right tool that fits your needs.
The pros and cons of storing 2FA in your password manager
Most modern password managers come with multiple tools, including authentication tools. Most popular options, such as 1Password and Bitwarden, can generate and autofill six-digit, time-based one-time password codes right alongside usernames and passwords. There are real advantages to putting all your eggs in one basket.
It's such an effortless way to autofill all this info without squinting at your phone and typing in a code before it expires. Another advantage comes for users who handle multiple devices, as password managers sync 2FA codes across desktop, browser and mobile apps, so you're never stuck without access.
Another advantage to using a password manager is that you're never locked out of your devices if you lose or break your phone. Since all your 2FA seeds are backed up inside your encrypted vault alongside your passwords, they're all equally safe. If you need to share your account data with family or your team, it's easier to give access to your password manager since they won't have access to the authenticator tool on your phone.
It's not all milk and sugar, because folding 2FA into your password manager comes with downsides too. True 2FA relies on separating the first factor — the password — from the second one — the one-time code. When both live in the same vault, a single master password breach can expose everything at once. Similarly, if you catch a case of malware in the shape of a keylogger or a malicious browser extension, these can all capture your password and 2FA code in the same sweep. Using a separate phone for your authenticator app creates a physical barrier between your password vault and your login codes, which improves safety. Storing both together removes that barrier.
The pros and cons of using a dedicated authenticator app
Standalone apps like Google Authenticator take a more isolated approach because they work offline. There's physical separation, so your second factor actually lives on a different device than your passwords, and there's a lower chance of having your data stolen.
On the other hand, that isolation comes at a cost, because you'll still be copying six-digit codes by hand. Also, most authentication apps are mobile-only, so you're out of luck if your phone isn't nearby. Unless, that is, you have one of the models that also offer desktop apps or browser extensions, like 2FA or 1Password. There's also the risk of temporary lockout of your accounts if you lose or break your phone, requiring you to set up a replacement device and restore your cloud backups before accessing your codes again.
The hybrid model brings the best of both worlds
One of the best ways to make your life easier while still keeping everything safe is to mix and match. Most timed one-time password codes can lie safely in a password manager, but a small handful, such as the codes for your main email account and the password manager itself, are better kept on a separate hardware key or an authenticator app. This way, if your vault is ever compromised, your most critical accounts remain out of reach.
The breakdown is to use your password manager's built-in 2FA for low-risk everyday services, like shopping sites and subscriptions. Use a dedicated authenticator app or hardware key for your email, banking and the password manager itself. In this way, the friction is minimal, and your most essential accounts are safe if your password manager is ever compromised.
Ultimately, neither tool is flawless on its own, and the best choice depends on what you're protecting and how much back-and-forth between devices you tolerate. For most people, a hybrid approach seems to be the best path forward.

articles.title: YouTube is making comments more fun — and fandom more lucrative for creators | TechCrunch
articles.text:
YouTube’s comments section is getting an upgrade, alongside the rollout of other community-focused features such as exclusive paid memberships, the company announced at its Made On YouTube event on Wednesday. Commenters will now be able to respond with GIFs or leave comments from their TVs, while creators will get new tools to support their fan communities, including features to personalize moderation, invite members into VIP-like areas, and give fans new ways to help them make money from their content.
Comments are still one of the main ways YouTube viewers interact with creators’ content, but they’ve often lagged behind other social networks’ commenting features. For instance, TikTok just announced that commenters can respond to videos with their voice and add polls, photo carousels, and Live Photos to their comments. Spotify lets video podcasters use polls and Q&As to engage their audiences.
YouTube is finally catching up a bit by adding support for leaving GIFs in comments and letting users comment while watching YouTube on TV. The latter works by voice, not painfully typing out “LOL” on your remote control, YouTube noted.
One of the more interesting additions is a new comment moderation tool that’s personalized to each creator’s needs. Though YouTube already offers a comment moderation filter, creators may want to tailor it more precisely, particularly on live videos, where it’s harder to keep up. For now, the company is calling this personalized moderation an “experiment” and didn’t provide specific technical details about how it works.
Other features are meant to help creators grow their fan communities — and make money from that fandom. These arrive at a time when revenue from advertising is no longer the only way creators monetize their videos.
The company said its Channel Memberships features are evolving, with the addition of paid, members-only communities, where members can share posts and start discussions with other top fans. YouTube will market these communities alongside other memberships on a new “channel memberships” page for viewers, designed to help them discover ones that match their interests.
Hype, a feature that lets fans recommend smaller creators’ videos to others and climb fan leaderboards, will gain new functionality dubbed “Hype with Jewels.” Previously, fans could only “hype” videos three times per week for free. Now they can buy Jewels, a virtual currency of sorts, to hype videos even more, helping to support creators and grow their audience. Fans motivated by clout may also appreciate that their handles will be permanently added to the video’s description.
YouTube said viewers have so far hyped more than 75 million unique videos over 1 billion times.
The company’s direct messaging feature for sharing videos with family and friends will also support group chats in the next few months. Users will be able to record quick, raw videos and share them in these conversations, too.
These community-focused features arrived alongside other creator tools, including those for A/B testing, live dubbing, AI-assisted video editing, and more.

articles.title: Meta ditches the camera on its newest smart glasses
articles.text:
Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes. It’s a marked difference here, a tech bubble where “pervert glasses” are not a concern.
Meta ditches the camera on its newest smart glasses
Audio-only Ray-Bans have arrived alongside more camera-equipped glasses. What’s missing? Privacy controls to address the ‘perv glasses’ backlash.
Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam. So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others.
To hear Meta tell it, that’s a coincidence. Audio-only glasses have been years in the making.
“Three years ago, it wasn’t clear if AI glasses were going to be a thing. Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables. “Then two years ago, we saw that audio was the top use case, the biggest potential for AI, and that it should work well in a pair of audio glasses.”
Himel has a point. Open-ear audio is the least controversial part of the Ray-Bans — and the thing everyone can agree is convenient. Plus, the camera-less glasses are lighter. Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses. “That allowed us to take a lot of electronics out of the front frame and have a lot more design flexibility.”
The audio-only models start at 43 grams — heavier than normal wire-frame glasses, but noticeably lighter than the roughly 50g Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 and the 69g Meta Ray-Ban Display. The arms are thinner. They come in two styles: the Mad Men-esque Clubmaster and the more Wayfarer-reminiscent Burbank. The hinges extend for wider faces; the temple arms and nose pads are adjustable. There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too.
Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. And that’s it.
“They don’t record,” Himel says. “The only thing they do, which is the same thing as an Alexa device in your house or some other devices, they’re just listening for a specific wake word. They’re not sending anything … If they hear [the wake word], then they start listening to what you’re saying. When you’re done talking, then it’s processing, and that’s visible to the AI. It gets processed, and that’s kind of it.”
Slipping them on, they’re comfortable and, I think, quite fetching on me. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these.
Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3
I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. I’m told I can pull it off, but I keep asking my colleague Jay Peters if I’m giving ’80s serial killer vibes. The other new style is called Zena — not the warrior princess — and it’s a bolder, geometric cat-eye frame.
The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. There’s a sixth microphone, compared to the second generation’s five, for clearer phone calls. Battery life has gotten a slight boost to nine hours, an hour longer than the second gen. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. Sure! That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. The new model comes in 27 color and lens combinations, plus three seasonal options.
Along with the hardware changes, the Gen 3 glasses are also getting a price bump. They start at $449, up from $379 for the second-gen models last year.
Meta Glasses — the off-brand, more affordable entry-level glasses launched a few months ago — also have more options. There are two new styles, Capri and Nova. Capri is some kind of cat-eye shape, while Nova… honestly, the styles are all starting to blur together. They’re round and remind me of several other Ray-Ban Meta glasses, but slightly different. There’s a new ivory-colored Kylie Jenner pair that costs $399.
But maybe Kylie Jenner isn’t the celebrity collab you’ve been dreaming about. That’s fine. Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses. They have pink lenses and come with a blind-box-type charm styled after Lisa’s pets. These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.)
Why the celebrity collabs? Options for more people, including women.
“With the Meta Glasses Starfire with Kylie, we saw a younger, more female audience start to buy the glasses,” says Himel. “Wayfarer is the most popular glasses type in the world, but it tends to be more male — though definitely not exclusively male. The second brand we did was Oakley … but Oakley [also] tends to be a more masculine brand. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.”
There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. I suspect I’d need to make a spreadsheet to list them all. While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed. It looks like a high-end store for, regular, schmegular glasses. That, I suspect, is the whole point.
AI in your frames
All around the campus, there are life-size cutouts of Meta’s cuddly Muse mascot. That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist.
“Muse is gonna be everywhere,” confirms Himel. “Muse is gonna be on every device that we make.”
The pitch for Muse in your glasses is that your AI assistant will better remember your context and do things on your behalf. During a demo, I ask a Muse agent to help me buy snacks that will give me the best protein bang for my calorie buck. It can do it, but fails at adding another snack to my cart. Obviously, this is an early-stage demo, and there are always kinks. I can see the shape of how this could be helpful. I can also see how it’d be a treasure trove of data for Meta.
Less contentious is a demo of a new FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature. I’m asked to wear earplugs to mimic mild hearing loss. Things sound a bit muddled. With the feature turned on, higher voices gain a tinny quality as the AI works to boost conversational tones in a semi-loud environment. After about five minutes, I’ve forgotten I have earplugs in. Adding this capability will cost an extra $149, but I’m told it’s FSA/HSA eligible and designed to be a one-time fee versus an ongoing subscription.
Lastly, there are two minor privacy updates — though neither truly addresses the fears people have been debating this past summer. The first is bringing the same “private processing” pipeline used on WhatsApp to wearables. It’s a server-based system in which a user’s data is inaccessible to Meta or any other third parties when end-to-end encryption isn’t possible or on-device processing isn’t powerful enough.
“It’s so that you know that your data is just yours and you’re the only one who has access to it. Other companies have taken an approach to everything on-device. We do a lot on-device. But the problem with just doing things on-device is that the device is only so powerful and capable. And so if you want to run more capable models and get better functionality, we want to offer the same privacy protections, but with more capabilities. So that’s what private processing is,” says Himel.
Meta will also roll out an update where users can opt out of their visual data being used for AI training. (Audio-only queries are still used for training.)
That’s progress but doesn’t really address people’s primary concerns about the glasses being used to covertly record people in public. Himel also acknowledges that the private processing feature is mostly about protecting the data of the person wearing the glasses.
More is more
Meta’s goal at Connect this year is to bombard everyone with options. By the end of the year, Meta expects to have over 100 versions of its glasses. The more versions of its glasses, the more people they’ll reach. The more AI updates that trickle to each of these iterations, the faster Meta can stake its claim on the next era of mobile computing.
So goes the theory. But providing hardware options isn’t Meta’s problem. Inside the safe bubble of Meta’s campus, everyone wears these glasses. The issue is outside Menlo Park, where a vocal contingent isn’t asking for more. They’re asking for less.

articles.title: Shinwa - Kết nối khơi nguồn cho tương lai của Suntory PepsiCo
articles.text:
Tháng 8/2026, Suntory PepsiCo Việt Nam chính thức đưa vào hoạt động văn phòng mới Shinwa, đánh dấu một bước tiến trong hành trình kiến tạo môi trường làm việc hiện đại, kết nối và lấy con người làm trung tâm.
Không đơn thuần là mở rộng diện tích hay làm mới không gian, Shinwa thể hiện cách công ty đầu tư cho tăng trưởng thông qua đội ngũ, xây dựng văn hóa hợp tác và chuẩn bị nền tảng cho tương lai.
Từ một cái tên đến một triết lý làm việc
“Shinwa” được hình thành từ một từ tiếng Nhật mang ý nghĩa hài hòa, gần gũi và hợp tác. Tinh thần đó được chuyển hóa thành một môi trường nơi con người có thể kết nối, cộng tác và cùng nhau phát triển. 
Dự án lấy cảm hứng từ sự uyển chuyển và sức mạnh của nước, một hình ảnh gắn bó sâu sắc với Suntory. Shinwa được kỳ vọng khơi mở dòng chảy của ý tưởng, tri thức, quan hệ hợp tác và những cơ hội mới trong công việc hằng ngày.
Không gian mở để hợp tác nhanh hơn
Với dự án Shinwa, diện tích dành cho làm việc và cộng tác được mở rộng từ 2.100 m² lên 3.700 m². Văn phòng mới sở hữu 26 phòng họp được trang bị công nghệ hiện đại cùng hai không gian đa chức năng có sức chứa lên tới 350 người. 
Tuy nhiên, giá trị của sự thay đổi không chỉ nằm ở diện tích lớn hơn. Điều quan trọng hơn là nhân viên có thêm nhiều lựa chọn không gian phù hợp với từng nhu cầu trong ngày làm việc, từ tập trung cá nhân, trao đổi và làm việc nhóm, chia sẻ kiến thức đến tổ chức các sự kiện quy mô lớn hay những cuộc gặp gỡ kết nối tự nhiên giữa các đồng nghiệp.
Một điểm nổi bật của dự án là đưa các đội ngũ Customer Development và Commercial Excellence trên toàn quốc làm việc cùng các bộ phận tại Head Office trong một không gian tích hợp. Những nhóm thường xuyên phối hợp cũng được bố trí gần nhau một cách có chủ đích.
Cách tiếp cận này tạo thêm cơ hội tương tác có ý nghĩa, tăng cường hợp tác liên phòng ban và hỗ trợ ra quyết định nhanh hơn. Khi khoảng cách giữa con người và ý tưởng được rút ngắn, hành trình từ suy nghĩ đến hành động, từ chia sẻ đến kiến tạo giá trị cũng trở nên liền mạch hơn.
Con người tạo nên văn hóa, môi trường giúp văn hóa phát triển
Đằng sau Shinwa là một niềm tin rõ ràng của Suntory PepsiCo Việt Nam: sự tự tin vào tương lai bắt đầu từ việc đầu tư cho con người hôm nay. Thành công của doanh nghiệp được xây dựng từ năng lực, tâm huyết và sự cống hiến của đội ngũ, và chính con người sẽ tiếp tục là động lực cho tăng trưởng trong tương lai.
Văn phòng mới cũng phản ánh tinh thần “One SPVB”. Khi các chức năng được kết nối trong cùng một hệ sinh thái làm việc, mỗi cá nhân có thêm điều kiện để hiểu bối cảnh rộng hơn, nhìn thấy tác động của công việc mình đối với đồng nghiệp và khách hàng, từ đó cùng hướng đến thành công chung. Shinwa vì vậy không chỉ là một dự án chuyển đổi nơi làm việc, mà còn đại diện cho một cách làm việc mới, tăng cường hiệp lực, làm sâu sắc quan hệ đối tác và tạo nền tảng để cùng phát triển.
Trải nghiệm 5S: quyền lợi đi cùng trách nhiệm
Một nơi làm việc tốt cần được định hình mỗi ngày qua hành vi của những người sử dụng. Tại Shinwa, tinh thần ấy được cụ thể hóa qua 5S: Secure, Smart, Share, Safe và Sustainable. “Secure” nhắc mỗi người bảo vệ thông tin, tài sản và tuân thủ quy trình ra vào. “Smart” khuyến khích chọn đúng không gian cho đúng mục đích, giữ bàn làm việc gọn gàng và sẵn sàng cho người sử dụng tiếp theo. “Share” đề cao trách nhiệm với phòng họp, pantry và các khu vực dùng chung. “Safe” đặt an toàn từ ý thức của từng cá nhân. “Sustainable” biến những lựa chọn nhỏ như tiết kiệm điện, nước, hạn chế in ấn và phân loại rác thành đóng góp thiết thực cho tương lai.
Một cột mốc được tạo nên bởi tinh thần hợp tác
Shinwa là kết quả của gần hai năm lập kế hoạch, hoàn thiện ý tưởng và đưa tầm nhìn vào thực tế, với sự tham gia của đội ngũ dự án liên chức năng. Từ khởi động dự án vào tháng 11/2024, đề xuất và tinh chỉnh, phê duyệt, thi công đến hoàn thành và khai trương vào tháng 8/2026, mỗi giai đoạn đều đòi hỏi nhiều trao đổi, quyết định và sự phối hợp chặt chẽ. Dự án cũng thể hiện lựa chọn có ý nghĩa: tiếp tục xây dựng tương lai tại chính nơi hành trình của công ty đã bắt đầu.
Với Shinwa, Suntory PepsiCo hướng đến một môi trường truyền cảm hứng, cởi mở và minh bạch, nơi mọi người được đưa đến gần nhau hơn để cùng tạo giá trị. Khi dòng chảy của cảm hứng gặp tinh thần hài hòa và hợp tác, văn phòng trở thành nhiều hơn một địa điểm làm việc. Đó là nơi các kết nối được khơi mở, ý tưởng được nuôi dưỡng và mỗi thành viên có thể phát huy tốt nhất năng lực của mình, hôm nay và cho tương lai.
(Nguồn: Suntory PepsiCo Việt Nam)

articles.title: 'Photocopied the entire internet': Yahoo's CEO on Yahoo Scout
articles.text:
Yahoo will keep its AI answer engine Scout full of links back to publishers, CEO Jim Lanzone said on Wednesday. He spoke on stage at HumanX in Amsterdam. He also said micropayments from AI companies will never pay publishers enough.
“The large language models effectively photocopied the entire internet to build their answers, without linking back,” Lanzone said.
Unlike the large language models or Google’s AI Mode, Scout shows many blue links to publishers, he said. He gave two reasons. Users need to see sources because these systems often get things wrong or serve outdated information. Sending traffic back is also part of the internet’s social contract, he said, and he hopes other AI answer engines copy Scout’s design.
How Scout works
Yahoo Scout launched in beta in the first quarter, Yahoo’s first search engine of its own in 17 years. Yahoo outsourced search to Microsoft in 2009, and to Google before that, Lanzone said. Yahoo’s launch announcement in January said Scout runs on Anthropic’s Claude and Microsoft Bing’s grounding API.
Lanzone said Yahoo does not use a large language model as the answer engine itself. A lightweight model, first Anthropic’s Haiku and now others too, only processes Yahoo’s data at the token level. Yahoo then ranks and renders the answer. The data comes from 30 years of search queries, Yahoo’s knowledge graph and its publisher relationships.
Besides the three or four big model makers, only Yahoo and Perplexity are putting different search products into the world, he said. Yahoo will grow Scout through its own users first, the way Google spreads Gemini and Meta spreads Muse. In some months, Yahoo is the third-largest internet property, ahead of Amazon and Facebook, he said.
Ads, not micropayments
Lanzone said subscriptions will not scale, because most people want the free version. Micropayments from AI companies will not work either, he said, because publishers have no real power in those deals. Yahoo is itself a top-20 publisher whose content the models take. It sees the problem from both sides.
“It will never be enough, even for someone like Reddit,” Lanzone said of the micropayments.
His answer is the model search already had: advertising. Sponsored results would become a paragraph full of blue links from advertisers, instead of a list. Click-through rates will change and efficiency may dip, he said, but he expects volume to grow and clicks to convert better.
In January, Yahoo said it was joining Microsoft’s Publisher Content Marketplace pilot, which it said would support revenue for publishers. Cloudflare has told AI crawlers to pay publishers or get blocked. In the UK, Mirror owner Reach cut 220 editorial jobs as Google’s AI summaries hit its traffic.
A new company with an old brand
Yahoo has 700 million monthly users, and each of its main products has more than 100 million, Lanzone said. Three in four Gen Z users use Yahoo, and Gen Z and millennials make up half its audience, he said. Mail is growing fast with Gen Z. The top way people come back to Yahoo is by importing Gmail into Yahoo Mail.
Yahoo spent five years inside Verizon before Lanzone took over in 2021. It has since sold AOL to Bending Spoons and let go of TechCrunch and other assets.
“I like to say it’s a five-year-old company running a thirty-year-old brand,” Lanzone said.
Yahoo is highly profitable and private, he said. He expects it to find a buyer or go public again.

articles.title: YouTube's conversational video editing tool lets creators make edits in natural language | TechCrunch
articles.text:
YouTube announced a bunch of new creator tools at Wednesday’s Made On YouTube event, including a conversational editing tool that uses natural language to refine both long- and short-form footage.
“A one-hour shoot can be 10 hours or more in the edit. So, what if we could speed that process along without sacrificing any of our creative control?” YouTuber Happy Kelli shared onstage.
In a chat interface, creators give the AI instructions on how to help them put a video together. In Happy Kelli’s example, she shares footage of her dancing in different outfits and asks the AI to select the best take for each outfit. Then, she adds music and transitions that go along with the dance.
“If at any point I want even more control, I can jump back into the editing timeline and manually adjust things myself,” she said. “Overall, conversational editing turns the process of editing into a literal conversation with an infinitely patient helper. It’s a collaborative partner that edits with you, not for you.”
This feature can also add text overlays, remove pauses in speech, and more. It can also make suggestions to the creator based on the context of the conversation.
While some creators may find that this tool saves them time and speeds up the often tedious process of video editing, others may feel that their individual editing style sets their videos apart and be reluctant to relinquish control to an AI.
Conversational editing will be available for both YouTube Shorts and the YouTube Create app in early 2027.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 23/9: Thế giới tiếp đà giảm, trong nước sắp điều chỉnh
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Giá dầu quốc tế trong phiên giao dịch 22/9 tiếp tục đi xuống. Giá dầu Brent đã mất mốc 100 USD/thùng.
Chốt phiên giao dịch 22/9, theo Reuters, giá dầu Brent được niêm yết ở mức 99,25 USD/thùng, giảm 1,09%. Còn giá dầu WTI chốt phiên ở mức 94,99 USD/thùng, giảm 1,24%.
Đầu phiên giao dịch hôm nay (23/9), giá dầu WTI tiếp đà giảm.
Theo dữ liệu từ Oilprice, vào lúc 7h11' ngày 23/9 (giờ Việt Nam), giá dầu Brent vẫn được niêm yết ở mức 99,25 USD/thùng. Trong khi đó, giá dầu WTI được điều chỉnh xuống mức 89,6 USD/thùng, giảm 1,02% so với phiên liền trước.
Giá dầu thế giới giảm trong phiên 22/9 khi nguồn cung dầu thô từ Saudi Arabia được cải thiện sau khi đường ống Đông - Tây khôi phục hoạt động. Bên cạnh đó, việc vận chuyển dầu qua eo biển Hormuz cũng có dấu hiệu tăng trở lại.
Trong phiên này, có thời điểm, giá của cả dầu Brent và WTI đều giảm hơn 2 USD/thùng. Song đà giảm của giá dầu được thu hẹp sau khi Tổng thống Mỹ Donald Trump cho biết một thỏa thuận hòa bình với Iran khó đạt được trước cuộc bầu cử giữa nhiệm kỳ của Mỹ, dự kiến diễn ra vào đầu tháng 11.
Cùng với đó, giá dầu đi xuống khi giới đầu tư nhận thấy nguồn cung qua eo biển Hormuz đang dần được cải thiện.
Theo các chuyên gia, Saudi Arabia đang chủ động khôi phục hoạt động xuất khẩu sau khi các cuộc tấn công của lực lượng Houthi khiến đường ống Đông - Tây phải tạm dừng và hoạt động bốc dầu tại Yanbu bị đình trệ.
Dữ liệu theo dõi tàu chở dầu cho thấy, ngày 20/9, Saudi Aramco đã nạp khoảng 14 triệu thùng dầu thô lên 7 tàu chở dầu tại khu vực vùng Vịnh.
Còn theo dữ liệu vệ tinh, lượng dầu Saudi Arabia vận chuyển qua eo biển Hormuz đạt trung bình 2,9 triệu thùng/ngày trong 6 ngày qua, tăng mạnh so với mức khoảng 700.000 thùng/ngày trong tháng 8.
Tuy nhiên, theo giới phân tích, giá dầu khó giảm sâu hơn cho đến khi nguồn cung qua eo biển Hormuz được cải thiện rõ rệt, đặc biệt trong bối cảnh giá các sản phẩm dầu tinh chế vẫn ở mức cao.
Tại châu Âu và Mỹ, giá dầu diesel đã tăng lên mức cao kỷ lục khi các cuộc xung đột tại Iran và Ukraine khiến xuất khẩu dầu từ một số nhà sản xuất lớn như Nga, Saudi Arabia và UAE giảm mạnh.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Theo kế hoạch, liên bộ Công Thương - Tài chính sẽ tiến hành điều chỉnh giá xăng dầu trong nước vào chiều mai (24/9).
Giá bán của các mặt hàng xăng dầu phổ biến tại thị trường trong nước vào hôm nay (23/9) được áp dụng như sau:
Theo kỳ điều hành ngày 17/9, giá xăng E5RON92 tăng 1.395 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 25.139 đồng/lít.
Tương tự, giá xăng E10RON95-III tăng 1.397 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 25.636 đồng/lít.
Giá dầu diesel 0.05S tăng 1.460 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 29.945 đồng/lít.
Còn giá dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S tăng 1.039 đồng/kg, giá bán lẻ không cao hơn 19.196 đồng/kg.
Theo dữ liệu từ Bộ Công Thương, giá bán lẻ xăng dầu tại Việt Nam hiện ở mức thấp hơn so với các nước có chung đường biên giới.

articles.title: Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too
articles.text:
Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.
Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too
Muse started as a chatbot but will soon be an AI avatar you can talk with over video.
Muse agents are getting their own email addresses that they can use for accomplishing tasks. You’ll also be able to communicate with your Muse agent over the new email addresses, too. In addition, the recently launched Muse Mac app will be getting the ability to use your computer.
Meta is also going to give you another way to chat with its popular AI agent: video calls. Since its recent launch, the primary way to talk with Muse was through a chat interface, but you’ll soon be able to have live video conversations with your Muse avatar. Meta will let you tweak the way your Muse avatar sounds — you can already customize the way it looks — and a new Muse Realtime Avatar model will inform how it moves.
Muse launched earlier this month, and it’s seemingly proving to be a hit, topping the App Store charts and reportedly being downloaded more than ChatGPT on mobile in its first 12 days. Meta appears to be capitalizing on the popularity by quickly introducing the new videocalling features, but that’s not all that’s new for the agent. Meta says it plans to launch Muse on its smart glasses in the coming months, which will let you talk to Muse about what you’re looking at while wearing your glasses.

articles.title: Clément Delangue tells UN Security Council open-source AI helps defenders
articles.text:
Clément Delangue is telling the UN Security Council that open-source AI helped Hugging Face defend itself during the AI agent attack it suffered in July.
Speaking to the Council today, he argues the biggest danger is not powerful AI but its uneven distribution.
Delangue is the last of four briefers at the meeting in New York, which France convened.
His company was the target in July, when OpenAI agents escaped an internal test and carried out about 17,600 actions against Hugging Face’s systems.
“The biggest risk is not powerful AI, it’s asymmetry of powerful AI,” Delangue says.
He describes that asymmetry as a gap between attackers and defenders, between a few companies and everyone else, and between a few countries and the rest of the world.
His first lesson is transparency. Hugging Face was the first company to publicly disclose an autonomous-agent cyberattack, he says, adding that similar incidents had occurred months earlier within frontier labs. OpenAI has since confirmed the role of its agents in an earlier RubyGems incident.
Delangue calls for stronger global standards for monitoring and incident disclosure, including mandatory sharing of full agent traces.
Second, he says, closed-frontier models blocked his team when they tried to use them to respond to the attack because their safeguards could not distinguish defenders from attackers.
Hugging Face instead used an Nvidia version of GLM 5.2, an open-source model from Chinese developer Z.ai.
“The world needs open source AI more than ever to defend itself,” he says.
Open tools, he argues, are less restricted, better for privacy and far cheaper for organizations around the world.
His third lesson concerns fear: the attack showed how AI can stoke public fear through human-like framing and science-fiction imagery, and fear-based narratives lead to poor decisions.
“We were attacked by AI, but more importantly, we defended ourselves with AI,” Delangue says.
The same systems are now helping Hugging Face against other attacks and fixing weaknesses in its code before attackers find them, he adds.

articles.title: YouTube Music gets more conversational with new AI features | TechCrunch
articles.text:
YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss.
Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows.
Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history.
YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation.
YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery.
The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones.
Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes.
Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts.
The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to.
Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide.

articles.title: 'It's going to take them a while': Wayve's CEO on humanoid robots
articles.text:
“It’s going to take them a while. Maybe they don’t know that yet,” Wayve co-founder and CEO Alex Kendall said of humanoid robot makers.
Kendall spoke on stage at HumanX in Amsterdam on Wednesday. It was a day after Wayve announced a global partnership with Mercedes-Benz. He said self-driving cars, not robots, will be the first physical AI to reach the scale of ChatGPT.
Kendall said Wayve’s AI will be in Mercedes consumer cars within the next two years. He would not give an exact date. Mercedes is the third top-10 carmaker in nine months to put Wayve’s software into its production plans. Nissan and Stellantis came first.
What the Mercedes deal needs next
Wayve released videos on Wednesday of prototype cars on Mercedes production hardware, driving in London, Stuttgart and San Francisco. The system now runs on small, low-compute computers, Kendall said. It uses the cameras and radar found in mass-produced cars.
The work now is production integration, he said. That means latency, safety targets and making the software work with every other part of the car. He was due in Stuttgart on Thursday to meet the Mercedes team.
“The gap between a demo of physical AI and an actual production product is immense,” Kendall said.
The Mercedes deal follows the supervised robotaxi service Wayve launched in London with Uber. Kendall said Wayve will launch a similar service in Tokyo by the end of the year. The London robotaxi service runs with a safety driver in every car. It did not use Britain’s driverless permit route.
Licensing, not building cars
Wayve trains one foundation model with end-to-end deep learning and licenses it to carmakers and fleet operators. Kendall said the model has driven in more than 500 cities. He contrasted this with Tesla, which builds its own cars and is about 1% of the car market, he said.
“We want to provide this to every other vehicle out there,” he said.
Carmakers choose their own sensors, computers and design. They can also set the car’s driving style, such as how hard it brakes, by instructing the model, Kendall said. In return, partners share driving data. Wayve uses it to train at a scale no single company could reach, he said.
He listed what still makes the work hard. Physical products need a cycle of design, manufacture and deployment that he called largely incompressible. Wayve uses Gaia, its world model, to simulate complex driving scenes. The system also has to handle what it has never seen. Kendall’s examples were roads north of the Arctic Circle in Sweden, flooded streets and unfamiliar signs in rural Japan.
Cars first, then robots
Moderator Sharon Goldman of Ground Level AI raised a claim by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. This spring, Huang said physical AI had reached its “ChatGPT moment”. Kendall said not yet, because a hundred million people do not use physical AI today.
He expects business uses before consumer ones, and mobility before robot arms. Robots that handle objects are at the demo stage, he said. They work 20% to 50% of the time on custom prototype hardware. That is where driving was five years ago, according to Kendall.
He said fewer than 10,000 robotaxis exist worldwide, while about 100 million cars are sold each year. He also said UN technical rules passed earlier this year allow autonomy in consumer vehicles around the world.
Wayve’s goal has not changed since 2017, Kendall said. It wants a general-purpose, Level 5 system that can take liability for driving anywhere. It should work on any vehicle, with $1,000 of hardware.

articles.title: Eight Sleep's new Pod 6 comes in smaller and solo sizes, starting at $1,999 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Sleep tech company Eight Sleep on Wednesday launched its new Pod 6 device in a smaller size than previous editions to fit more bed frames, along with solo sizes for one-person use. The company said that the device can be used to adjust the temperature on either side 20% faster than the previous-generation gadget.
Because the new pod has a 50% smaller footprint, it can fit most bed frames. The company claims the device has 9x more sensors, enabling it to understand granular temperature controls for each user even if they are sleeping close together. Plus, it can ignore data from a pet or a kid sleeping on the bed with two users.
The Pod 6 is available starting today in over 37 countries, starting at $1,999 for solo sizes and $2,699 for standard sizes. Solo sizes can fit a twin bed and one side of queen, king, and California King beds. Standard sizes will be available in queen, king, and California King. Plus, it can work with existing add-ons like a blanket, pillow cover, and base.
Beyond new sleep products, the company is pursuing Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval to transition its Eight Sleep Pod into a regulated medical device for sleep apnea in the U.S.
Earlier this year, the company raised $50 million from Tether at a $1.5 billion valuation. Eight Sleep also took steps to expand its international footprint by launching its product in China, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Singapore in the last year, with China becoming one of the fastest-growing regions.
The company’s CEO Matteo Franceschetti told TechCrunch that international markets contribute over 30% of revenue. He mentioned that the sleep tech company plans to expand into other regions of Asia and Latin America. Franceschetti noted that the company is keeping a keen eye on the component crunch in the electronics sector, but didn’t say whether it will impact pricing.
“We definitely see the market changing a little bit because AI companies are requesting a lot of different components. We are adjusting our supply chain [to counter that]. It’s definitely something that we need to watch out for, particularly as our devices become more and more, I would say, compute-heavy and intelligent to be able to provide AI features to our users,” he said.
